messages.content: Describe a foggy winter evening in Delhi, in about 70 words.

By six in the evening, a thick fog has swallowed the city. Streetlights glow like blurry yellow moons, and cars crawl along with their hazard lights blinking. People hurry home with mufflers wrapped over their noses. At the corner, a group of rickshaw pullers warms their hands over a small fire. The smell of roasted peanuts and wood smoke hangs in the cold air. Sounds seem softer, as if the whole city is whispering.
Write a simple poem, 4 lines, about a sleepy cat in the sun.

The cat lies down in a golden beam,
And blinks her eyes as if in a dream.
She stretches long and gives a yawn,
Then purrs herself to sleep till dawn.
In around 75 words, describe a mountain lake covered in morning fog.

The lake lies silent under a thick white blanket of fog. You cannot see the other shore, only the dark outlines of pine trees that seem to float in the air. The water is still, like glass. A single duck glides through the mist and leaves a thin ripple behind. Cold air touches your cheeks, and everything sounds soft and far away. Slowly, the sun rises, and the fog lifts like a curtain.
Write a story, around 85 words, for primary school children about two friends who quarrel over a toy and then solve the problem.

Sameer and Raju both loved the red toy truck. One day, they pulled it so hard that a wheel came off. "You broke it!" cried Sameer. "No, you did!" said Raju. They sat far apart and did not talk. Soon, they felt sad and lonely. Then Raju picked up the wheel and said, "Shall we fix it together?" They found some glue and worked side by side. The truck rolled again, and both boys smiled. After that, they took turns playing with it.
Please write a story, about 100 words, about two neighbours who built a wall between their houses and then made a little door in it.

Two neighbours quarrelled over a mango tree, and one of them built a high wall between their houses. For months they did not speak. One day a ball from one garden flew over the wall and landed in the other. The boy next door knocked on the wall, calling for his ball. Nobody answered. His father felt sorry and took a small hammer. By evening there was a little wooden door in the wall. The other neighbour came through it with the ball and a mango. They both laughed, and shared the fruit.
School library notice, please: it will be closed on Thursday for stocktaking and will reopen on Friday. About 35 words. Sign it Librarian.

NOTICE
The school library will be closed on Thursday for stocktaking. It will reopen on Friday. Please plan your visits accordingly. We apologise for the inconvenience. Thank you for your understanding.
Librarian
Invite my uncle to my piano recital on Sunday at 5 pm. Keep it warm and short, about 45 words. I'm Meghna.

Dear Uncle,
I am playing in my piano recital this Sunday at 5 pm, and I would love for you to be there. It would mean a lot to me to see you in the audience. I'm a little nervous, but excited too. Please do come!
With love,
Meghna
Prepare a story, about 80 words, about a village that has no clock. A boy makes a sundial, and the story ends with everyone meeting at the same time.

In a small village, nobody owned a clock. People met whenever they pleased, and meetings were always late. One day, a boy named Gopal noticed that the shadow of a tall pole moved slowly across the ground. He pushed a stick into the ground and marked the line where the shadow fell at noon. Soon, he added more marks. He had made a sundial. The villagers were amazed. Next morning, everyone gathered by the sundial together at the same time.
Write a short rhyming verse, around 45 words, about being brave on the first day at a new place.

My heart goes thump, my steps are slow,
I do not know the way to go.
But I will smile and take a chance,
And soon my fear will learn to dance.
A friendly face will say hello,
And then I'll feel the courage grow.
Write one paragraph, 55 words, about why trees are like quiet friends.

Trees are like quiet friends. They give us shade when the sun is harsh and fruit when we are hungry. They hold the soil in place and give homes to birds. They never ask for anything, and they stand with us year after year. All we have to do is look after them in return.
Hopeful, with a little humour: a farmer waiting for rain.

Farmer Gopal looked at the sky every morning, and every morning the sky looked back at him, blue and empty. He had sown his rice, and the seedlings were turning brown.

His wife, Revati, told him to stop staring. "Staring does not make it rain."

"Neither does washing the cow," said Gopal, but he wiped his face and went to look at the field. He wore his oldest hat, for luck.

The next afternoon, a single cloud appeared, then four. The cow lowed. A gust of wind snatched his hat and carried it into the paddy.

The rain came while he was still chasing it. He caught the hat at last. His wife ran out with a pot on her head, and the two of them stood laughing in the downpour while the field drank.
How does a boy get the whole class quiet by whistling a tune? Tell it as a story.

The Class 7 room was as noisy as a market. The substitute teacher, Mr. Kishore, tried shouting, but it only made things worse. At the back of the room, a boy named Prasad cleared his throat and began to whistle a slow, gentle tune, the kind his grandfather played on the fields. One by one, the chatter faded. A few heads turned. By the time he reached the second line, every face was calm, and the whole room had gone quiet. Mr. Kishore, astonished, waited until the tune ended. "Thank you," he said. "Please do that again every time I need you." Prasad grinned. He whistled for the rest of the year.
Fashion a story about a boy who was mean to his friend and finds a kind way to say sorry.

Bipin laughed when his friend Ashok tripped over his own bag and everyone looked. Ashok did not laugh. He picked up his things and walked off without a word. Bipin felt a stone settle in his chest. The next day, Ashok avoided him in class. Bipin thought hard about what to do. At lunch, he walked up to Ashok's desk and quietly put down a small paper boat. Inside it, he had written, "I should not have laughed. Can you forgive me?" Ashok read the note, folded the boat into a pocket and said, "Next time, help me pick up the books." Bipin nodded and promised.
About 120 words, please: a boy loses his school shoe in the mud.

During the rainy season, Anwar's left shoe came off in the mud outside the school gate, and no amount of pulling brought it back. He hopped around on one foot, soaking his sock. A group of Class 6 girls came by and laughed, and he turned red. A girl named Jaya, however, found a long stick and began poking the mud near his foot. Another girl found a second stick, and together they dug until the sole appeared. Anwar pulled out the shoe, covered in brown sludge, and shook it triumphantly. They washed it under the tap. He walked into class with one very clean shoe, one muddy sock and a loud, happy squelch with each step.
Make up two friends who meet outside the exam hall and exchange good luck charms.

Outside the Class 10 exam hall, Rasheed and Ketaki stood in the queue, both pale. Rasheed was holding a small green pencil he used for luck. Ketaki had a tiny brass elephant in her pocket. They spotted each other and burst into nervous laughter. "Swap?" said Rasheed. She nodded, and they traded. He took the elephant with a bow, and she tucked the pencil behind her ear. Inside, the paper was hard, and both of them felt the funny weight of the other's charm in their hands. Afterwards, they met on the steps and compared notes. "Elephants do not forget," Rasheed said, holding up the answer sheet. They exchanged the charms back and agreed to repeat it next time.
Narrate a story about a girl who lights a lamp for her grandmother on the first Diwali after she is gone.

The first Diwali without Ajji felt wrong. Tanya's house was quiet, and her mother had not made any sweets. Tanya found Ajji's old brass lamp in the cupboard. She polished it for an hour until it shone. Then she filled it with oil and set it by the door. When she lit the wick, a gentle flame rose. Her mother came and stood beside her. They said nothing for a while. Then her mother began to cry, and Tanya hugged her. After a while, they walked to the kitchen and made a small batch of Ajji's favourite sweet, kneading the dough together.
Pen a tale about a sugar cane juice seller and a hot afternoon.

Ganesh pressed sugar cane through his old iron machine and filled glasses with green juice and a squeeze of lime. It was a very hot afternoon, and the line was long. A delivery boy on a bike pulled up, sweating. He had no money left, only a few coins. Ganesh looked at his flushed face. "Take a glass," he said. The boy drank it in one go. "I'll pay tomorrow," he said. The next day, he came back and not only paid but also brought two friends. By evening, Ganesh had sold three hundred glasses and could not feel his arm.
Could you invent a tale about a clock tower that gave away spare minutes?

The clock tower in Dharampur had a secret. Every evening at six, it let a few spare minutes drip from its hands like honey.

Most people never noticed. But a boy named Yash, who was always late, caught one in his palm. It was warm and tiny, shaped like a seed.

"What's this?" he asked.

"A spare minute," said the tower, with a deep gong. "Use it well."

The next morning, Yash was running behind again. He remembered the seed and let it open. Time seemed to stretch. He tied his shoes, packed his bag, and had a moment left over to wave to the dog.

He reached school early. Then he came to the tower every evening and held out both hands.
Two raindrops race down a window. Write the story.

Drip and Drop were two raindrops sliding down the window of a school bus. They had agreed to race to the bottom.

"Ready, steady, go!" said Drip.

They slid. Drip went straight. Drop wobbled left, then right. A tiny speck of dust caught him.

"Wait!" Drop called. "I'm stuck!"

Drip paused. Winning would be easy now, but it felt lonely. So he slid back up a bit and joined Drop, and together they grew heavy and round, and rolled past the dust.

At the bottom of the window, they reached the edge at the very same moment and dripped off together onto the road.

A girl on the bus, named Zara, had been watching. She smiled, because it was a tie.
Help me write a diary entry of about 100 words about my grandmother visiting us after a long time.

Dear Diary,
Nani came to stay with us today after almost two years. The moment she walked in, the whole house smelled of the laddoos she had brought from her village. She looked a little smaller than I remembered, but her laugh was just as loud. After dinner, we sat on the terrace, and she told me stories about Ma as a naughty little girl. I laughed so much my stomach hurt. She is staying for three weeks, and I already know it will feel too short. Tomorrow she has promised to teach me her pickle recipe.
